steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for a paper on few-shot adaptation of large vision-language models like CLIP. Explain the problems with current prompt- and adapter-based efficient transfer learning, especially their reliance on per-task hyperparameter tuning, motivate a validation-free setting, introduce our CLAP method, and list our contributions.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Large vision-language models and the cost of adapting them
- Efficient transfer learning: prompts vs adapters
- Overfitting and hyperparameter dependence of adapter methods
- Limits of task-specific model selection
- Our realistic setting, ZS-LP baseline and CLAP
- Contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- VLMs
  - CLIP: reshaping research landscape, unprecedented performance
  - trained on hundreds of millions of image-text pairs via contrastive learning
  - remarkable zero-shot performance thanks to rich representations
  - heavy hardware/data demands -> trained only on singular occasions
  - large scale -> full fine-tuning impractical on small few-shot downstream tasks
- ETL: prompts vs adapters
  - add small set of learnable parameters optimized during adaptation
  - visual or text prompts in input space; adapters across network
  - prompt learning backpropagates through entire network: burden on resource reuse, no black-box adaptation, possible source data leakage (privacy)
  - adapters: gradients only on extra params (typically last layer); no costly fine-tuning or leakage; state-of-the-art performance
- Overfitting / hyperparameters
  - challenge: improve target task while preserving generalization
  - severe overfitting to support set; updated prototypes deviate from zero-shot prototypes
  - CLIP-Adapter, TIP-Adapter carefully adjust model-specific + scheduler hyperparameters to control trade-off
  - recent evidence: apparently use large-scale test set to adjust hyperparameters
- Limits of model selection
  - hyperparameters don't generalize across tasks (Fig. 1)
  - SoTA can't find homogeneous configuration beating well-initialized Linear Probing (LP)
  - realistic scenario: degradations up to 21% vs this baseline
  - biased model selection; large labeled set + case-specific tuning unrealistic, impractical (grid-search per case)
  - selection not based solely on support samples -> method incomplete, impractical
- Our setting and CLAP
  - strict but realistic: only support samples accessible
  - no evaluation subset -> adapters need robust model selection strategy
  - ZS-LP (weights initialized with CLIP zero-shot prototypes) strong baseline, beats convoluted ETL
  - penalize large deviations from zero-shot prototypes
  - issues: scalar penalty uniform across classes (hurts harder classes); weight needs validation set
  - CLass-Adaptive linear Probe (CLAP), Augmented Lagrangian Multiplier approach
- Contributions
  - observation: per-task tuning needed; fixed configuration underperforms ZS-LP
  - penalty term; modified ALM; balancing weight learned in outer iteration; i) class-wise multipliers (class prototypes, data augmentation), ii) one outer-step update, no validation set
  - experiments: 11 benchmarks, domain generalization, full fine-tuning comparison, ablations; consistent with homogeneous configuration

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large vision-language models (VLMs) such as CLIP are changing the research landscape because of their unprecedented performance. These models are trained on a very large dataset of hundreds of millions of image-text pairs, which are used through contrastive learning. Once they are trained, VLMs have remarkable zero-shot performance on a wide range of visual recognition problems, thanks to the rich representations they learn. But this training needs a lot of hardware and data resources, which suggests these models can only be trained on singular occasions. Also, because these networks are so large, adjusting their parameters on small downstream tasks with only a few labeled samples is hard, and fully fine-tuning the whole model is impractical.

An alternative that is emerging to deal with this is to fine-tune VLMs by adding a small set of learnable parameters and optimizing their values during the adaptation step. These tunable weights can be put in the input space as visual or text prompts, or added as adapters across the network. Both families of approaches belong to the Efficient Transfer Learning (ETL) literature, but prompt learning still needs to backpropagate gradients through the whole network. So, besides being a burden on resource reuse, these methods do not allow black-box adaptation, and this raises a possible concern about leaking the source data, which is very important in privacy-oriented applications. Adapter-based strategies, on the other hand, only need gradients on the extra parameters, usually in the last layer. This avoids costly fine-tuning and data leakage, and still gives state-of-the-art performance.

Adapter-based methods for fine-tuning VLMs in the few-shot learning paradigm have made progress, but it is still a challenge to improve performance on the target task and keep their generalization capabilities at the same time. We argue this is probably because of severe overfitting to the support set samples used in few-shot adaptation, which moves the updated class prototypes far away from the zero-shot prototypes that the pre-trained model initially gives. Popular adapter-based ETL strategies like CLIP-Adapter and TIP-Adapter carefully tune model-specific hyperparameters, together with other key hyperparameters of the learning scheduler, to control the trade-off between the initial zero-shot inference and integrating new information from the support set. In addition, recent evidence suggests that these works apparently use the large-scale test set to tune their hyperparameters.

There is a significant limitation here: when these hyperparameters are optimized for one task, they do not generalize well to other tasks, as Fig. 1 shows. State-of-the-art (SoTA) methods struggle to find a homogeneous configuration that does better than a simple well-initialized Linear Probing (LP) adaptation. In a realistic adaptation scenario (Fig. 1), we can see dramatic drops in performance, up to 21%, compared to this simple baseline. These practices basically bias the model selection process. Assuming access to a much larger set of labeled samples and adjusting the model hyperparameters case by case is not only unrealistic but also impractical (grid-search has to be done for each case). So we argue that if the model selection strategy of an ETL method is not based only on the support samples, the method is incomplete and impractical for real-world few-shot adaptation problems.

- Our setting and CLAP
  - only support samples accessible; no evaluation subset -> need robust model selection
  - ZS-LP (init with CLIP zero-shot prototypes) strong baseline, beats convoluted ETL
  - penalize large deviations from zero-shot prototypes
  - issues: scalar penalty uniform across classes; balancing weight needs validation set
  - CLass-Adaptive linear Probe (CLAP), Augmented Lagrangian Multiplier approach
- Contributions
  - per-task tuning observation; fixed config underperforms ZS-LP
  - penalty term + modified ALM; class-wise multipliers; one outer-step update
  - experiments: 11 benchmarks, domain generalization, full fine-tuning comparison, ablations

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:

These tunable weights can be put in the input space as visual or text prompts, or added as adapters across the network. Both families of approaches belong to the Efficient Transfer Learning (ETL) literature, but prompt learning still needs to backpropagate gradients through the whole network. So, besides being a burden on resource reuse, these methods do not allow black-box adaptation, and this raises a possible concern about leaking the source data, which is very important in privacy-oriented applications. Adapter-based strategies, on the other hand, only need gradients on the extra parameters, usually in the last layer. This avoids costly fine-tuning and data leakage, and still gives state-of-the-art performance.

We argue this is probably because of severe overfitting to the support set samples used in few-shot adaptation, which moves the updated class prototypes far away from the zero-shot prototypes that the pre-trained model initially gives. Popular adapter-based ETL strategies like CLIP-Adapter and TIP-Adapter carefully tune model-specific hyperparameters, together with other key hyperparameters of the learning scheduler, to control the trade-off between the initial zero-shot inference and integrating new information from the support set. In addition, recent evidence suggests that these works apparently use the large-scale test set to tune their hyperparameters.

There is a significant limitation here: when these hyperparameters are optimized for one task, they do not generalize well to other tasks, as Fig. 1 shows. State-of-the-art (SoTA) methods struggle to find a homogeneous configuration that does better than a simple well-initialized Linear Probing (LP) adaptation. In a realistic adaptation scenario (Fig. 1), we can see dramatic drops in performance, up to 21%, compared to this simple baseline. These practices basically bias the model selection process. Assuming access to a much larger set of labeled samples and adjusting the model hyperparameters case by case is not only unrealistic but also impractical (grid-search has to be done for each case). So we argue that if the model selection strategy of an ETL method is not based only on the support samples, the method is incomplete and impractical for real-world few-shot adaptation problems.

In this work we want to redirect the efforts in few-shot ETL to a stricter but realistic scenario, where only the support samples can be accessed during training. Since there is no evaluation subset, new adapters need to include a model selection strategy that is robust across a large spectrum of tasks. We observed empirically that a carefully designed Linear Probing (ZS-LP), with weights initialized with the zero-shot prototypes from CLIP, is a strong baseline that outperforms more convoluted ETL solutions. To improve the ZS-LP baseline further and optimize the trade-off between the initial zero-shot representations and the updated class prototypes on new tasks, we propose to penalize large deviations from the original zero-shot prototypes during adaptation. But the learning objective we get has two major issues. First, the penalty that controls the deviation between the original and updated prototypes is a scalar value, the same for all classes, and this can hurt the model's performance when there are harder-to-learn classes. Second, the penalty balancing weight has to be set with a validation set, which conflicts with our validation-free scenario. To address these limitations we propose CLass-Adaptive linear Probe (CLAP), which is based on an Augmented Lagrangian Multiplier approach. Our contributions are:

- We observe empirically that SoTA few-shot ETL adapters need careful adjustment of a set of key hyperparameters for each task, which is unrealistic and impractical in real-world settings. Surprisingly, if one fixed configuration is used across tasks, these methods are likely to do much worse than a simple Linear Probing strategy initialized with the zero-shot prototypes from CLIP.

- We propose a principled solution for the trade-off between original and updated class prototypes in Linear Probing, which adds a penalty term to penalize large deviations from zero-shot prototypes. To deal with the challenges of the resulting constrained optimization problem, we present a modified Augmented Lagrangian Multiplier (ALM) method. This removes the need to fine-tune the penalty balancing weight, which is learned in the outer iteration of the optimization process. To adapt ALM to this scenario we made two critical choices: i) using class prototypes, as well as data augmentation, motivates using class-wise multipliers, instead of sample and class-wise multipliers as in the original ALM; ii) in this scenario there is no validation set, and the only feedback available is from the support samples, so we only do one outer-step update, which can avoid potential overfitting on the support set.

- We give extensive experiments to assess the performance of CLAP in the proposed scenario, including few-shot adaptation on 11 popular classification benchmarks, domain generalization, comparison to full fine-tuning methods, and ablation studies to validate our choices. As shown in Fig. 1 and in the experimental section, CLAP gives consistent performance across different tasks with a homogeneous configuration, and outperforms SoTA ETL approaches by a large margin in all scenarios.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large vision-language models (VLMs), such as CLIP [1], are reshaping the research landscape with their unprecedented performance. These models are trained on an extensive dataset of hundreds of millions of image-text pairs, leveraged via contrastive learning [1]. Once trained, VLMs offer remarkable zero-shot performance on a wide span of visual recognition problems thanks to their rich learned representations [1,2]. Nevertheless, the extensive hardware and data resources that such training demands [3] suggest that these models can only be trained on singular occasions. Furthermore, the large scale of these networks makes it challenging to adjust their parameters on small downstream tasks involving only a few labeled samples, rendering full fine-tuning of the entire model impractical.

An emerging alternative to alleviate this issue consists in fine-tuning VLMs by adding a small set of learnable parameters whose values are optimized during the adaptation step [4,5,6,7,8]. These tunable weights can be introduced in the input space as visual [5] or text prompts [4,6], or added in the form of adapters across the network [7,8,9]. While both families of approaches fall within the Efficient Transfer Learning (ETL) literature, prompt learning still requires backpropagating gradients through the entire network. Thus, besides burdening resource reuse, these methods preclude black-box adaptation, raising a potential concern about leaking the source data, which is paramount in privacy-oriented applications. In contrast, adapter-based strategies only need gradients on the extra set of parameters, typically in the last layer, avoiding costly fine-tuning and data leakage while yielding state-of-the-art performance [9,10].

Despite the progress of adapter-based methods for fine-tuning VLMs under the few-shot learning paradigm, improving performance on the target task while preserving generalization capabilities remains a challenge [4]. We argue that this is likely due to severe overfitting to the support set samples used during few-shot adaptation, which makes the updated class prototypes deviate significantly from the zero-shot prototypes initially provided by the pre-trained model. In fact, popular adapter-based ETL strategies, such as CLIP-Adapter [7] and TIP-Adapter [8], carefully adjust model-specific hyperparameters, along with other key hyperparameters of the learning scheduler, to control the trade-off between initial zero-shot inference and the integration of new information from the support set. Furthermore, recent evidence [10] suggests that these works apparently use the large-scale test set to adjust their hyperparameters.

A significant limitation is that these hyperparameters, when optimized for one specific task, do not generalize well to other tasks, as illustrated in Fig. 1. Indeed, state-of-the-art (SoTA) methods struggle to find a homogeneous configuration that outperforms a simple well-initialized Linear Probing (LP) adaptation. In a realistic adaptation scenario (Fig. 1), we observe dramatic performance degradations of up to 21% compared to this simple baseline. These practices bias the model selection process, since assuming access to a significantly larger set of labeled samples and adjusting the model hyperparameters case by case is not only unrealistic but also impractical (grid-search must be done for each case). We therefore argue that if an ETL method’s model selection strategy is not based solely on the support samples, the method is incomplete and impractical for real-world few-shot adaptation problems.

In this work, we seek to redirect few-shot ETL efforts towards a stricter but realistic scenario in which only the support samples are accessible during training. Without an evaluation subset, novel adapters must include a model selection strategy that is robust across a large spectrum of tasks. Interestingly, we empirically observed that a carefully designed Linear Probing (ZS-LP), whose weights are initialized with the zero-shot prototypes from CLIP, is a strong baseline that outperforms more convoluted ETL solutions. To further improve ZS-LP and optimize the trade-off between initial zero-shot representations and updated class prototypes on novel tasks, we propose penalizing large deviations from the original zero-shot prototypes during adaptation. The resulting learning objective, however, presents two major issues. First, the penalty controlling the deviation between original and updated prototypes is a scalar value, uniform across all classes, which can hurt the model’s performance on harder-to-learn classes. Second, the penalty balancing weight must be set using a validation set, which conflicts with our validation-free scenario. To address these limitations, we propose CLass-Adaptive linear Probe (CLAP), based on an Augmented Lagrangian Multiplier approach. Our contributions can be summarized as follows:

- • We empirically observe that SoTA few-shot ETL adapters require careful adjustment of a set of key hyperparameters for each task, which is unrealistic and impractical in real-world settings. Surprisingly, if a fixed configuration is adopted across tasks, these methods are likely to substantially underperform a simple Linear Probing strategy initialized with CLIP's zero-shot prototypes.

- • We propose a principled solution to the trade-off between original and updated class prototypes in Linear Probing, which integrates a penalty term on large deviations from the zero-shot prototypes. To address the challenges of the resulting constrained optimization problem, we present a modified Augmented Lagrangian Multiplier (ALM) method. This removes the need to fine-tune the penalty balancing weight, which is instead learned in the outer iteration of the optimization process. Adapting ALM to this scenario required two critical choices: i) leveraging class prototypes, as well as data augmentation, motivates class-wise multipliers instead of the sample and class-wise multipliers of the original ALM; ii) since there is no access to a validation set and the only feedback comes from the support samples, we perform only one outer-step update, which can avoid potential overfitting on the support set.

- • We provide extensive experiments assessing CLAP in the proposed scenario, including few-shot adaptation on 11 popular classification benchmarks, domain generalization, comparison to full fine-tuning methods, and ablation studies validating our choices. As shown in Fig. 1 and in the experimental section, CLAP delivers consistent performance across tasks with a homogeneous configuration and largely outperforms SoTA ETL approaches in all scenarios.

References:
[1] Alec Radford, Jong Wook Kim, Chris Hallacy, Aditya Ramesh, Gabriel Goh, Sandhini Agarwal, Girish Sastry, Amanda Askell, Pamela Mishkin, Jack Clark, et al. Learning transferable visual models from natural language supervision. In International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML) , pages 8748–8763, 2021.
